p: Kuntillet Ajrud, also known by the Hebrew name Horvat Teman, was one of the few water sources along the Darb el-Ghazza, the Gaza Road, which ran from the site of ancient Eilat or Ezion-Geber past Kuntillet Ajrud and Kadesh Barnea up to Gaza. Carbon-14 dating indicates that the site was occupied from 801 to 770 BCE.

The main building is fortress-like and divided into two rooms, one large and one small, both with low benches. Both rooms held paintings and inscriptions on the walls and on two large water jars, or pithoi, one found in each room.

What the site was for is disputed. It is frequently described as a shrine, though this is not certain. The excavator, Ze'ev Meshel, first argued for a religious function from the inscriptions and drawings with religious themes and from an unusual amount of linen, which he connected with the dress of priests. Other scholars point out that the site has no temple, shrine or cultic objects, and that similar textiles have since been found at Kadesh Barnea. Four inscriptions carry the military title Commander of the Fortress, three on storage jars and one on the plastered walls, which supports the view that it was a state-sponsored fortress or a caravanserai.

Although its position in the Sinai would normally point to the Kingdom of Judah, the occupants are usually taken to have come from the northern Kingdom of Israel. The evidence is the pottery, the personal names with the ending -yaw, the northern spelling of some inscriptions and the references to Yahweh of Samaria.

Edward Henry Palmer identified the place in 1869, when it was known as Contellet Garaiyeh, with the station Gypsaria on the Tabula Peutingeriana, and noted the remains of an ancient fort. Ze'ev Meshel of Tel Aviv University excavated it in 1975 and 1976, and the excavation report was published in 2012.

The paintings on the pithoi show animals, stylised trees and human figures. They appear to have been made over a considerable period by several artists and form no coherent scenes. Talley Ornan has argued that all the drawings have parallels in Neo-Assyrian palace reliefs and were preliminary sketches for wall paintings, and Schniedewind has read the inscriptions as scribal exercises of soldiers stationed at the fortress. Mordechai Gilula's theory that two figures on one jar represent Yahweh and the goddess Asherah has been almost abandoned: the scholars who have analysed the images in most detail hold that they are Bes or Bes-like figures.

notes: The article gives Schniedewind (and Smoak, Hadley) by surname only, so the text names Schniedewind without a first name.
The article calls the occupants 'Israelian' (northern Israel); I wrote 'from the northern Kingdom of Israel'.
Occupation dates 801-770 BCE are the article's carbon-14 range; the existing description says c. 800 BCE.
